back: A growth response of part of a plant to a stimulus coming from one direction: towards it is positive, away from it is negative.
A growth response in which parts of a plant grow towards or away from the direction of light. Shoots are positively phototropic.
A growth response in which parts of a plant grow towards or away from gravity. Roots are positively gravitropic; shoots are negatively gravitropic.

front: Why are tropisms useful to a plant?
back: Shoots grow towards light for photosynthesis; roots grow down to anchor the plant and reach water and mineral ions.

front: What do foil-cap and tip-removal experiments show?
back: The shoot tip detects the light and produces the growth substance; the bending happens just below the tip.
Rotates a seedling slowly so that gravity (or light) acts equally on all sides, removing the one-sided stimulus. It does not remove gravity.
Auxin made in the shoot tip diffuses back, collects on the shaded side and stimulates more cell elongation there, so the shoot bends towards the light.

front: Why does a horizontal shoot curve upwards? (Supplement)
back: Auxin collects on the lower side, which elongates more, so the shoot curves up (negative gravitropism).
A chemical made in small amounts in one part of a plant and carried to other parts, where it controls growth and development.
Auxins: rooting powder, selective weedkillers. Gibberellins: larger seedless grapes, faster germination. Cytokinins: tissue culture. Ethylene: ripening fruit.

front: Which plant hormone is a gas, and what does it do? (ZIMSEC)
back: Ethylene (ethene): it promotes fruit ripening and the fall of leaves and fruit.
